questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent
questions.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{7}{25-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{7}{25}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{25-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{7}{25}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{7}{25}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 5\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{7}{5}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{7}{5}\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{7}{5}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{5})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x}{5}|<1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine
questions.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $25{x}^{2}=(5x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{\pi }}{\sqrt{25{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{{e}^{\pi }}{\sqrt{(5x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{\pi }\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{5}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{{e}^{\pi }}{5}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡5x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent
questions.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $25{x}^{2}={(5x)}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{10}{1-25{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =10\int \frac{1}{1-(5x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =2\operatorname{artanh}⁡5x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|5x|<1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
questions.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{3}{\sqrt{256{x}^{2}-16}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{16{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $16{x}^{2}=(4x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=4x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $4$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{3}{\sqrt{256{x}^{2}-16}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{(4x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{16}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{3}{16}\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u{|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{16}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡4-\operatorname{arcosh}⁡2)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
questions.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
{\int }_{2}^{5}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x=2{\int }_{2}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $(2x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $2$ | $5$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $4$ | $10$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{5}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{2}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{4}^{10}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{10}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u\,{|}_{4}^{10} \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(10)-\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(4) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(10+\sqrt{{(10)}^{2}-1})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(4+\sqrt{{(4)}^{2}-1}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(10+\sqrt{99})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(4+\sqrt{15}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{10+\sqrt{99}}{4+\sqrt{15}})\end{aligned}
$$
